subject: unbounded distance sampling and gamma function

messages.author: 509d884113938f54
messages.subject: unbounded distance sampling and gamma function
parts:
A colleague has a data set of transects sampled using distance sampling.  There are three bands: 0-25m, 25-100m, >100m.  I think I read somewhere that Andy's 2004 distance sampling model (distsamp) and/or Richard's generalization of that model (gdistsamp) can handle unbounded outer bands.  Is that the case?  Must the model be generalized first or can the model handle unbounded outer bands in its current state?

My colleague currently is only using the two innermost bands and is finding that there are >3x as many counts in the 25-100m band than in the 0-25m band.  This, of course, could mean birds are being scared away from the observer or that habitat in the second band is preferred.  Regardless, it also seems to suggest that detection probability increases with distance and is causing her models to crash.

We are wondering whether distsamp or gdistsamp can use the gamma detection function.  The idea is that with three bands and the gamma detection function perhaps detection probability will be allowed to increase from the first band to the second band and then decrease in the third band.

Alternatively, perhaps Andy's 2004 N-mixture model could be used since there are two transects per site.  Band could be a categorical covariate in lambda.  That seems very straight-forward.

However, the idea of using distance sampling with the unbounded third band is the preferred approach.  Especially, if a gamma detection function could be used to allow detection probability to increase with distance and then decrease.  Since there are two transects per site and these transects could be considered replicate samples, perhaps gdistsamp can be used or perhaps Andy's latest Bayesian model in The Auk could be used?

Thank you for any suggestions.

Mark

messages.subject: AW: [unmarked] unbounded distance sampling and gamma function
parts:
Dear Mark,

 

this may be very much a dirty trick, but I wonder whether you couldn't simply set some maximal distance beyond which very few if any of the birds are likely to have been detected. Of course, this would have to be done on a per-species basis (and perhaps stratified for different habitats).

 

I take it that they did not collect the exact distance data but only the binned data are available ? This is always unfortunate, because then you are stuck with these bins.

 

Regards  ---Marc

Hi,

 

I just wanted to comment on this:
This, of course, could mean birds are being scared away from the observer or that habitat in the second band is preferred.

It is always good to make sure the assumptions of the model aren’t being violated too seriously. One assumption made when using distance sampling methods is that “objects are detected at their initial location prior to any movement in response to the observer”. Maybe someone else with more experience can comment on how important/flexible this assumption is in the grand scheme of things, but thought it was worth noting.

 

Chris

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] unbounded distance sampling and gamma function
parts:
hi Chris et al.,
 
 I 2nd what Richard said: you expect more birds in the middle distance bands using point counts just due to the geometry of the situation.
 With regard to Chris' comment: I think movement away from the observer really messes things up badly although I can't think of a specific study. But clearly it should lead to over-estimating abundance.
 
 We did a study with really wide distance bands (100 m) arguing that while there was movement (in that case toward the observer) it was mostly influencing nearby individuals and so they were in the same distance band they started out in (the paper is Sillett et al. 2012; Ecol Apps).
 
regards
andy

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] unbounded distance sampling and gamma function
parts: One other point. If you wanted to explicitly account for animal movement away from the transect, you would need to relax the "uniformity" assumption. In other words, you would need to model the expected number of individuals occurring in each distance bin. You couldn't do this by using a different detection function such as one that resembles a gamma distribution.

parts:
Thanks, Richard and Andy.  I probably should not have mentioned possible movement away from the observer because I do not know that happened.

My primary reason for posting was to ask whether distsamp or gdistsamp allows for inclusion of unbounded third bands and whether it is possible to incorporate the gamma detection function to model an increase and then a decrease in detection probability.

The field design did not use point counts, but rather line transects.  My apologies for not being clear about that.

I have derived the cell probabilities for Andy's 2004 distance sampling model and for Richards 2011 availability model.  I thought I might try to derive the cell probabilities for gdistsamp and allow for unbounded third bands.  But before I attempted to do that I thought I would ask if it has already been done for either distsamp or gdistsamp.

If I can derive the cell probabilities for unbounded bins (without known distances to individual birds) using the distsamp or gdistsamp models perhaps I can try to add the gamma function.

Mark





On Tuesday, November 11, 2014 4:54:39 PM UTC, Richard Chandler wrote:
One other point. If you wanted to explicitly account for animal movement away from the transect, you would need to relax the "uniformity" assumption. In other words, you would need to model the expected number of individuals occurring in each distance bin. You couldn't do this by using a different detection function such as one that resembles a gamma distribution. 

On Tue, Nov 11, 2014 at 11:40 AM, Jeffrey Royle <jar...@gmail.com> wrote:
hi Chris et al.,
 
 I 2nd what Richard said: you expect more birds in the middle distance bands using point counts just due to the geometry of the situation.
 With regard to Chris' comment: I think movement away from the observer really messes things up badly although I can't think of a specific study. But clearly it should lead to over-estimating abundance.
 
 We did a study with really wide distance bands (100 m) arguing that while there was movement (in that case toward the observer) it was mostly influencing nearby individuals and so they were in the same distance band they started out in (the paper is Sillett et al. 2012; Ecol Apps).
 
regards
andy
 

On Tue, Nov 11, 2014 at 10:14 AM, Chris Sutherland <chris...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi,

 

I just wanted to comment on this:

 

This, of course, could mean birds are being scared away from the observer or that habitat in the second band is preferred.

 

It is always good to make sure the assumptions of the model aren’t being violated too seriously. One assumption made when using distance sampling methods is that “objects are detected at their initial location prior to any movement in response to the observer”. Maybe someone else with more experience can comment on how important/flexible this assumption is in the grand scheme of things, but thought it was worth noting.

 

Chris

Is it point transect/count or line transect data? For point count data, you would expect more detections in the 25-100m interval than in the 0-25m interval because the area is much larger. The model accounts for this.

Dear Mark,

 

this may be very much a dirty trick, but I wonder whether you couldn't simply set some maximal distance beyond which very few if any of the birds are likely to have been detected. Of course, this would have to be done on a per-species basis (and perhaps stratified for different habitats).

Von: unma...@googlegroups.com [mailto:unma...@googlegroups.com] Im Auftrag von Mark W. Miller
Gesendet: Dienstag, 11. November 2014 14:48
An: unma...@googlegroups.com
Betreff: [unmarked] unbounded distance sampling and gamma function

 

A colleague has a data set of transects sampled using distance sampling.  There are three bands: 0-25m, 25-100m, >100m.  I think I read somewhere that Andy's 2004 distance sampling model (distsamp) and/or Richard's generalization of that model (gdistsamp) can handle unbounded outer bands.  Is that the case?  Must the model be generalized first or can the model handle unbounded outer bands in its current state?

 

My colleague currently is only using the two innermost bands and is finding that there are >3x as many counts in the 25-100m band than in the 0-25m band.  This, of course, could mean birds are being scared away from the observer or that habitat in the second band is preferred.  Regardless, it also seems to suggest that detection probability increases with distance and is causing her models to crash.

 

We are wondering whether distsamp or gdistsamp can use the gamma detection function.  The idea is that with three bands and the gamma detection function perhaps detection probability will be allowed to increase from the first band to the second band and then decrease in the third band.

 

Alternatively, perhaps Andy's 2004 N-mixture model could be used since there are two transects per site.  Band could be a categorical covariate in lambda.  That seems very straight-forward.

 

However, the idea of using distance sampling with the unbounded third band is the preferred approach.  Especially, if a gamma detection function could be used to allow detection probability to increase with distance and then decrease.  Since there are two transects per site and these transects could be considered replicate samples, perhaps gdistsamp can be used or perhaps Andy's latest Bayesian model in The Auk could be used?

 

Thank you for any suggestions.

 

Mark

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: unbounded distance sampling and gamma function
parts:
Something seems off here.

The expected number of individuals in the second bin (25-100m) should be 3x that for the first bin (0-25m) if the data are from a line transect.  For a circular point count, E[N] for the second bin jumps to 15x that for the first bin, again because of geometry.  But this is all for E[N], not E[y|N].  If detection decreases with distance, then E[y|N] should be lower than E[N] in those second bins.

What Mark described with these count data makes it sound like detection probability does not exhibit a decrease with distance out to 100m.  Hence the model will have trouble determining the form of the detection function.  Otherwise, maybe detection does decrease with distance but this getting confounded with movement by individuals out of the first distance band.

Either way it seems that the repeated survey will be most useful at describing detection probability.

messages.author: 509d884113938f54
messages.subject: Re: unbounded distance sampling and gamma function
parts:
Thank you, Dan.

My suspicion is that detection probability increases from the center line to somewhere in the second band and then decreases further outward.  This can happen in the absence of any movement (for example, if habitat is dense near the line and becomes open in the middle band).  I suppose it could also happen by random chance.

My questions are:

1. do the distance sampling models in unmarked allow for an unbounded outermost band when distance to individuals is not known?

2. can a gamma function be used to model detection when detection is highest at an intermediate distance?

Perhaps nobody knows the answer to the second question and I am prepared (or perhaps preparing myself) to explore the answer to that question.

The study design did not use point counts.  The study design used line transects.

Thanks again for the reply.

Mark

That is not what happened in my case, and is unrelated to my questions.  Nevertheless, it seems to me that this could generate the observed pattern very easily.

Mark
